title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 828–830 (Night 181, continuing nights-180), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 181 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Dahnash and Maymūna lay the princess Budūr beside the sleeping Qamar al-Zamān and uncover both faces: the two are so alike that they might be twins, and the narrator quotes two poets on such a pair. Dahnash swears his beloved is the lovelier; Maymūna calls him blind in eye and heart, kisses Qamar al-Zamān between the eyes, and recites a fourteen-line ode in his praise, ending on the claim that there is a Joseph in every part of his beauty. Dahnash is moved to delight and wonder at her verse. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyatu wa-al-thamānūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the first and-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eighty-first night,
sentences.n: al-ḥādiya, “the first”, is the ordinal that compound numbers use in place of al-ūlā; it agrees with al-layla, and the tens, al-thamānūna, follow in the same nominative case. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْعِفْرِيتَ دَهْنَشَ وَالْعِفْرِيتَةَ مَيْمُونَةَ لَمْ يَزَالَا حَامِلَيْنِ الْمَلِكَةَ بُدُورَ حَتَّى نَزَلَا وَمَدَّاهَا بِجَانِبِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ʿifrīta Dahnasha wa-al-ʿifrītata Maymūnata lam yazālā ḥāmilayni al-malikata Budūra ḥattā nazalā wa-maddāhā bi-jānibi Qamari al-Zamāni ʿalā al-sarīri
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-ifrit Dahnash and-the-she-ifrit Maymūna not ceased (being) two-carrying the-queen Budūr, until the-two-came-down and-the-two-stretched-her-out at-(the)-side (of) Qamar al-Zamān on the-bed.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the ifrit Dahnash and the she-ifrit Maymūna carried the Princess Budūr on until they came down and laid her out beside Qamar al-Zamān on the bed.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the thread by repeating the last sentence of the night before. This time the verb follows its subjects, so it is dual: lam yazālā, “the two did not cease”, with ḥāmilayni, “carrying”, as its accusative predicate. al-malika is literally “the queen”, the title of a king's daughter here, al-Malika Budūr; Budūr, “full moons”, is a woman's name and so a diptote: Budūra. The shadda of مدّاها is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَكَشَفَا عَنْ وُجُوهِ الِاثْنَيْنِ فَكَانَا أَشْبَهَ النَّاسِ بِبَعْضِهِمَا
sentences.tr: wa-kashafā ʿan wujūhi al-ithnayni fa-kānā ashbaha al-nāsi bi-baʿḍihimā
sentences.l: And-the-two-uncovered from (the) faces (of) the-two, and-the-two-were (the) most-alike (of) the-people to-some-of-them-two.
sentences.i: They uncovered the faces of the pair, and the two were more like each other than any two people alive.
sentences.n: kashafa ʿan, “to lay bare”: the verb takes ʿan for what is uncovered. wujūh, “faces”, is plural where two faces are meant, as Arabic often has it. ashbah bi-, “more like”: the bi- marks the one resembled, and bi-baʿḍihimā, literally “to some of the two of them”, is “to one another”.

sentences.t: فَكَأَنَّهُمَا تَوْأَمَانِ أَوْأَخَوَانِ مُنْفَرِدَانِ وَهُمَا فِتْنَةٌ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِمَا الشَّاعِرُ الْمُبِينُ —
sentences.tr: fa-kaʾannahumā tawʾamāni aw-akhawāni munfaridāni wa-humā fitnatun li-al-muttaqīna ka-mā qāla fīhimā al-shāʿiru al-mubīnu —
sentences.l: So-as-if-they-two (were) twins or-two-brothers standing-apart, and-they-two (were) a-temptation for-the-God-fearing, as said about-them-two the-poet, the-clear-spoken —
sentences.i: They might have been twins, or two brothers set apart from all the world, and the pair of them were a temptation to the God-fearing, as the eloquent poet said of them:
sentences.n: ka-anna, “as if”, takes the pronoun suffix -humā, “the two of them”. The ء of توأمان is printed. او اخوان, aw akhawāni, “or two brothers”, is set solid in the print as one word, and is pointed here as one; akhawāni is the dual of akh, “brother”, and keeps the run of duals going: tawʾamāni … akhawāni munfaridāni. munfarid, “alone, standing apart”: set apart from all others, without peer. fitna is “trial, temptation”: beauty enough to lead even the pious astray; li- marks the ones it tempts. al-muttaqūn are those who guard themselves against God's displeasure. ka-mā, “as”: ka-, “like”, with mā, “what”. al-mubīn, “clear-spoken, eloquent”, from abāna, “to make plain”. The dash is the print's.

sentences.t:
يَا قَلْبُ لَا تَعْشَقْ مَلِيحًا وَاحِدًا * تَحْتَارُ فِيهِ تَذَلُّلًا وَتَدَلُّلَا
وَاهْوِ الْمِلَاحَ جَمِيعَهُمْ تَلْقَاهُمُ * اِنْ صَدَّ هٰذَا كَانَ هٰذَا مُقْبِلًا
sentences.tr:
yā qalbu lā taʿshaq malīḥan wāḥidan * taḥtāru fīhi tadhallulan wa-tadallulā
wa-ihwi al-milāḥa jamīʿahum talqāhumu * in ṣadda hādhā kāna hādhā muqbilā
sentences.l:
O heart, do-not love a-comely-one single, * (that) you-be-at-a-loss in-him, abasement and-coquetry;
and-love the-comely-ones, all-of-them, you-meet-them: * if turned-away this-one, was this-one coming-toward-(you).
sentences.i:
O heart, do not love one fair one alone, to be lost in him, all abasement while he plays the coquette;
love all the fair, and you will meet them all: if this one turns away, that one is coming toward you.
sentences.n: The print has وتذللا, a misprint for وتدللا, corrected here. Metre: kāmil, rhyming in -lā. The pointing is otherwise the print's own. tadhallul, “abasement, self-humbling”, and tadallul, “coquetry, coy airs”, differ by one dot and make a pair: the lover's abasement against the beloved's airs. The print points the imperative واهو as ihwi, as though from hawā, yahwī, “to fall”; the verb “to love” is hawiya, yahwā, whose imperative is ihwa, and “love” is plainly the sense. talqāhumu, “you will meet them”, stands where the answer to an imperative is usually jussive (talqahum); the extra -u fills the metre. After in, “if”, kāna has a present sense: “this one is coming toward you”. At the rhyme, -an is read -ā.
al-ākhar, “the other”, here “another (poet)”. The آ of الآخر is printed.

sentences.t: رَايْتُ بِعَيْنِي نَائِمَيْنِ عَلَى الثَّرَى * وَدَدْتُهُمَا لَوْ يَرْقُدَانِ عَلَى جَفْنِي
sentences.tr: raʾaytu bi-ʿaynī nāʾimayni ʿalā al-tharā * wadadtuhumā law yarqudāni ʿalā jafnī
sentences.l: I-saw with-my-eye two-sleeping-ones upon the-earth; * I-wished-them-two that they-two-would-lie upon my-eyelid.
sentences.i: I saw with my own eye two lying asleep on the ground; I wished that they might lie upon my eyelid.
sentences.n: Metre: ṭawīl, rhyming in -nī. The pointing is the print's own, and it prints رايت with no hamza: read raʾaytu, “I saw”. The ئ of نائمين is printed. bi-, “with”, marks the instrument. al-tharā is the moist earth, the ground. wadadtuhumā, “I wished them”, is pointed wadadtu as printed, where wadidtu is the commoner form; wadda … law, “to wish that”: after a verb of wishing, law brings in the wish. To keep someone “on the eye” is to hold them dearest, and the lover's eyelid, which knows no sleep, would make the sleepers a bed.

sentences.l: And-became Dahnash and-Maymūna (the two) looking at-them-two.
sentences.i: Dahnash and Maymūna stood gazing at the pair.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “to fall to, set about”. The verb is singular before its two subjects; yanẓurāni, after them, is dual.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ دَهْنَشُ وَاللّٰهِ طَيِّبٌ يَا سَيِّدَتِي إِنَّ مَحْبُوبَتِي أَحْسَنُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Dahnashu wa-Allāhi ṭayyibun yā sayyidatī inna maḥbūbatī aḥsanu
sentences.l: So-said Dahnash: By-God, good, O my-lady; indeed my-beloved (is) more-beautiful.
sentences.i: Then Dahnash said, “By God, he is fine, my lady, but my beloved is the fairer.”
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- of oaths, with the genitive after it. ṭayyib, “good, fine”: Dahnash grants the youth his due before claiming more for his own; the word is still the everyday “all right” of spoken Arabic.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ مَيْمُونَةُ بَلْ مَعْشُوقِي أَحْسَنُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu Maymūnatu bal maʿshūqī aḥsanu
sentences.l: So-said to-him Maymūna: Nay, my-beloved (is) more-beautiful.
sentences.i: Maymūna said to him, “No, my beloved is the fairer.
sentences.n: bal, “nay, rather”, sets aside what was said and puts the speaker's own claim in its place.

sentences.t: وَيْلَكَ يَا دَهْنَشُ أَنْتَ أَعْمَى الْعَيْنِ وَالْقَلْبِ مَا تُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ الْغَثِّ وَالسَّمِينِ
sentences.tr: waylaka yā Dahnashu anta aʿmā al-ʿayni wa-al-qalbi mā tufarriqu bayna al-ghaththi wa-al-samīni
sentences.l: Woe-to-you, O Dahnash! You (are) blind (of) the-eye and-the-heart; not you-distinguish between the-lean and-the-fat.
sentences.i: Woe to you, Dahnash! You are blind in eye and heart alike, and cannot tell the lean from the fat.
sentences.n: waylaka, “woe to you”. aʿmā al-ʿayni, “blind of eye”: the adjective is narrowed by the noun after it. mā with the imperfect, “not”, negates the present; it is Classical as well as spoken, and the plain negative of the edition. al-ghathth wa-al-samīn, “the lean and the fat”, is a proverbial pair for the worthless and the good. The shadda of الغثّ is the print's own.
تخفى is the print's spelling of tukhfī, “you hide”, with ى for final ي, a habit of the edition; it is pointed as written. hal asks a yes-or-no question, here as a reproach.

sentences.t: أَمَا تَنْظُرُ إِلَى حُسْنِهِ وَجَمَالِهِ وَقَدِّهِ وَاعْتِدَالِهِ
sentences.tr: a-mā tanẓuru ilā ḥusnihi wa-jamālihi wa-qaddihi wa-iʿtidālihi
sentences.l: Do-not you-look at his-handsomeness and-his-beauty and-his-stature and-his-symmetry?
sentences.i: Do you not see his loveliness and his beauty, his stature and his fine proportions?
sentences.n: a-mā, the question particle a- with mā, “not”: “do you not …?”. qadd, “stature, figure”, and iʿtidāl, “evenness, symmetry”, are a standing pair in descriptions of beauty, and iʿtidālihi rhymes with jamālihi. The shadda of وقدّه is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَيْلَكَ اسْمَعْ مَا أَقُولُهُ فِي مَحْبُوبِي
sentences.tr: waylaka ismaʿ mā aqūluhu fī maḥbūbī
sentences.l: Woe-to-you, hear what I-say-it about my-beloved,
sentences.i: Woe to you, listen to what I say of my beloved,
sentences.n: mā aqūluhu, “what I say”: the -hu points back to mā. fī, “in”, here “about, concerning”.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ كُنْتَ مُحِبًّا صَادِقًا لِمَنْ تَعْشَقُهَا فَقُلْ فِيهَا مِثْلَ مَا أَقُولُ فِي مَعْشُوقِي
sentences.tr: wa-in kunta muḥibban ṣādiqan li-man taʿshaquhā fa-qul fīhā mithla mā aqūlu fī maʿshūqī
sentences.l: and-if you-are a-lover true to-whom you-love-her, then-say about-her (the) like (of) what I-say about my-beloved.
sentences.i: and if you are a true lover of the one you adore, then say as much of her as I say of mine.”
sentences.n: li-man, “of the one whom”: li- marks whom the lover (muḥibb) loves. man has no gender of its own; the -hā of taʿshaquhā, “you love her”, shows a woman is meant. fa- brings in the answer to the condition, here an imperative.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ مَيْمُونَةَ قَبَّلَتْ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ قُبَلاً عَدِيدَةً وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْقَصِيدَةَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Maymūnata qabbalat Qamara al-Zamāni bayna ʿaynayhi qubalan ʿadīdatan wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-qaṣīdata
sentences.l: Then indeed Maymūna kissed Qamar al-Zamān between his-two-eyes kisses numerous, and-she-recited, saying, this the-ode:
sentences.i: Then Maymūna kissed Qamar al-Zamān between the eyes, kiss upon kiss, and recited this ode:
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”, is the narrator's usual way of moving on; inna puts Maymūna in the accusative. qubal is the plural of qubla, “a kiss”. The shadda of قبّلت and the vowels of قُبلاً are the print's own. anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”: the imperfect describes the reciting. A qaṣīda is an ode, a longer poem on a single rhyme.

sentences.t:
مَالِيْ وَلِلَّاحِيْ عَلَيْكَ يُعَنِّفُ * كَيْفَ السُّلُوُّ وَاَنْتَ غُصْنٌ اَهْيَفُ
لَكَ مُقْلَةٌ كَحْلَاءُ تَنْفُثُ سِحْرَهَا * مَا لِلْهَوَى الْعُذْرِيِّ عَنْهَا مَصْرِفُ
تُرْكِيَّةُ الْاَلْحَاظِ تَفْعَلُ بِالْحَشَا * مَا لَيْسَ يَفْعَلُهُ الصَّقِيلُ الْمُرْهَفُ
حَمَّلْتَنِي ثِقْلَ الْغَرَامِ وَاِنَّنِيْ * بِالْعَجْزِ عَنْ حَمْلِ الْقَمِيصِ وَاَضْعَفُ
وَجْدِيْ عَلَيْكَ كَمَا عَلِمْتَ وَلَوْعَتِيْ * طَبْعٌ وَعِشْقِيْ فِيْ سِوَاكَ تَكَلُّفُ
لَوْاَنَّ قَلْبِيْ مِثْلَ قَلْبِكَ لَمْ اَبِتْ * وَالْجِسْمُ مِنِّيْ مِثْلَ خَصْرِكَ مُنْحِفُ
وَيْلَاهُ مِنْ قَمَرٍ بِكُلِّ مَلَاحَةٍ * بَيْنَ الْاَنَامِ وَكُلِّ حُسْنٍ يُوصَفُ
قَالَ الْعَوَاذِلُ فِى الْهَوَى مَنْ ذَا الَّذِيْ * اَنْتَ الْكَئِيبُ بِهِ فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ صِفُوا
يَا قَلْبَهُ الْقَاسِي تَعَلَّمْ عِطْفَةً * مِنْ قَدِّهِ فَعَسَى يَرِقُّ وَيَعْطِفُ
لَكَ يَا اَمِيرِيْ فِى الْمَلَاحَةِ نَاظِرٌ * يَسْطُو عَلَيَّ وَحَاجِبٌ لَا يَنْصِفُ
كَذَبَ الَّذِيْ ظَنَّ الْمَلَاحَةَ كُلَّهَا * فِيْ يُوسُفٍ كَمْ فِيْ جَمَالِكَ يُوسُفُ
اَلْجِنُّ تَخْشَانِيْ اِذَا قَابَلْتُهَا * وَاَنَا اِذَا اَلْقَاكَ قَلْبِيْ يَرْجُفُ
اَتَكَلَّفُ الْاِعْرَاضَ عَنْكَ مَهَابَةً * وَاِلَيْكَ اَصْبُو جَهْدَ مَا اَتَكَلَّفُ
وَالشَّعْرُ اَسْوَدُ وَالْجَبِينُ مُشَعْشَعٌ * وَالطَّرْفُ اَحْوَرُ وَالْقِوَامُ مُهَفْهَفُ
sentences.tr:
mā lī wa-li-al-lāḥī ʿalayka yuʿannifu * kayfa al-sulūwu wa-anta ghuṣnun ahyafu
laka muqlatun kaḥlāʾu tanfuthu siḥrahā * mā li-al-hawā al-ʿudhriyyi ʿanhā maṣrifu
turkiyyatu al-alḥāẓi tafʿalu bi-al-ḥashā * mā laysa yafʿaluhu al-ṣaqīlu al-murhafu
ḥammaltanī thiqla al-gharāmi wa-innanī * bi-al-ʿajzi ʿan ḥamli al-qamīṣi wa-aḍʿafu
wajdī ʿalayka ka-mā ʿalimta wa-lawʿatī * ṭabʿun wa-ʿishqī fī siwāka takallufu
law-anna qalbī mithla qalbika lam abit * wa-al-jismu minnī mithla khaṣrika munḥifu
waylāhu min qamarin bi-kulli malāḥatin * bayna al-anāmi wa-kulli ḥusnin yūṣafu
qāla al-ʿawādhilu fī al-hawā man dhā alladhī * anta al-kaʾību bihi fa-qultu lahum ṣifū
yā qalbahu al-qāsī taʿallam ʿiṭfatan * min qaddihi fa-ʿasā yariqqu wa-yaʿṭifu
laka yā amīrī fī al-malāḥati nāẓirun * yasṭū ʿalayya wa-ḥājibun lā yanṣifu
kadhaba alladhī ẓanna al-malāḥata kullahā * fī Yūsufin kam fī jamālika Yūsufu
al-jinnu takhshānī idhā qābaltuhā * wa-anā idhā alqāka qalbī yarjufu
atakallafu al-iʿrāḍa ʿanka mahābatan * wa-ilayka aṣbū jahda mā atakallafu
wa-al-shaʿru aswadu wa-al-jabīnu mushaʿshaʿun * wa-al-ṭarfu aḥwaru wa-al-qiwāmu muhafhafu
sentences.l:
What (is it) to-me and-to-the-blamer (who) over-you chides? * How (can there be) consolation, and-you (are) a-bough slender?
For-you (is) an-eye kohl-dark (that) breathes-out its-magic; * not for-the-love, the-ʿUdhrite, from-it (is) a-turning-away.
Turkish (of) the-glances, it-does to-the-entrails * what not does-it the-burnished, the-keen-edged.
You-have-laden-me (with the) weight (of) passion, and-indeed-I, * in-the-incapacity for carrying the-shirt, (am) and-weaker.
My-longing for-you (is) as you-know, and-my-burning * (is) nature, and-my-love for other-than-you (is) affectation.
If-that my-heart (were) like your-heart, not would-I-pass-the-night * and-the-body of-me like your-waist, wasted.
Woe-is-me from a-moon with-every grace * among mankind, and-every beauty (that) is-described!
Said the-blamers about the-love: Who (is) this whom * you (are) the-grieving over-him? So-I-said to-them: Describe!
O his-heart, the-hard, learn a-bending * from his-figure; so-perhaps it-will-soften and-incline.
For-you, O my-emir, in the-beauty (is) an-eye (that) * assails me, and-a-brow (that) not does-justice.
Lied he-who thought the-beauty, all-of-it, * (was) in Joseph: how-many in your-beauty (is) a-Joseph!
The-jinn fear-me when I-face-them, * and-I, when I-meet-you, my-heart trembles.
I-force-myself (to) the-turning-away from-you (out of) awe, * and-toward-you I-yearn, (for all the) effort (of) what I-force-myself.
And-the-hair (is) black, and-the-brow radiant, * and-the-eye dark-and-lustrous, and-the-stature slender.
sentences.i:
What have I to do with the blamer who chides me over you? How can I forget you, when you are a slender bough?
You have an eye, dark as with kohl, that breathes out its spells: chaste ʿUdhrī love itself has no escape from it.
Its glances are Turkish: they do to the heart what no keen and polished blade can do.
You have laden me with the weight of passion, and I, who have not the strength to bear a shirt, am weaker still.
My longing for you is as you know, and my burning is my nature; love for any but you would be a pretence.
Were my heart like your heart, I would not lie the night through with my body wasted thin as your waist.
Alas for a moon that holds every grace among mankind, and every beauty that words can tell!
The censurers said of my love, “Who is he, that you grieve so for him?” And I said to them, “Describe him!”
O that hard heart of his, learn some bending from his supple frame: then perhaps it will soften and lean my way.
My prince, in your beauty there is an eye that bears down on me, and a brow that never deals justly.
He lied who thought all beauty lay in Joseph: how many Josephs there are in your beauty!
The jinn fear me when I meet them face to face, and I, when I meet you, my heart trembles.
I force myself in awe to turn away from you, and yet I yearn toward you, for all my forcing.
The hair is black, the brow is radiant, the eye dark and lustrous, the figure slender.
sentences.n: Metre: kāmil, rhyming in -fu. The pointing is the print's own. Line 1: mā lī wa-li-X, “what have I to do with X?”: li- marks each party to the question. al-lāḥī, “the blamer”, the stock figure who reproaches the lover; sulūw is forgetting a love, finding consolation; ahyaf, “slender-waisted”. Line 2: muqla, “eye”; kaḥlāʾ, “dark-lidded as if with kohl”; nafatha, “to breathe out”, as a sorcerer blows on knots. al-hawā al-ʿudhrī is chaste love, named for the Banū ʿUdhra, a tribe whose lovers were said to die of love; li- marks the one who has (or lacks) something: “ʿUdhrī love has no turning from it”. Line 3: the Turks were the archers of the age, and the glances strike like their arrows. faʿala bi-, “to do (something) to”: bi- marks what is acted on; al-ḥashā, the inward parts, seat of love's pain. al-ṣaqīl al-murhaf, “the burnished, the keen-edged”, is the sword, named by its epithets alone. Line 4: the second half runs stiffly, “and I, in my incapacity for bearing a shirt, and weaker”; the sense is a lover too weak to bear even a shirt's weight. It is kept as printed. Line 5: ṭabʿ, “innate nature”, against takalluf, “forced effort, pretence”. Line 6: لواَنّ, law-anna, “if it were that”, is set solid in the print as one word. The beloved's heart is hard and his waist slim: the lover has the slimness and lacks the hardness. munḥif is printed as an active participle, where munḥaf, “made thin”, might be expected; it is kept. Line 7: qamar, “moon”, is the stock image for a lovely face, and here it also sounds the youth's name, Qamar al-Zamān, “moon of the age”. bi-, “with”: a moon endowed with every grace. Line 8: the ʿawādhil, “censurers”, are the blamer's company; al-kaʾīb bihi, “grieving over him”: bi- gives the cause. ṣifū, “describe!”: whatever beauty they describe will be his, for he is “every beauty that is described”. The ئ of الكئيب is printed. Line 9: the poem turns to speak of him in the third person. ʿiṭfa, “a bend, a sway”, plays on yaʿṭifu, “to incline in kindness”: let his heart learn from his swaying body to bend toward the lover. Line 10: a court pun. nāẓir is “eye” and also “overseer, minister”; ḥājib is “eyebrow” and also “chamberlain”, the officer who keeps petitioners from the prince: so the beloved is addressed as amīr, “my prince”, and his features are his officials. The print points يَنْصِفُ as a Form I verb; the sense wants Form IV, lā yunṣifu, “does not deal justly”; the print's vowels are kept. Line 11: Joseph (Yūsuf), whose story is told in the twelfth sura of the Qurʾān, is the proverbial type of male beauty. Yūsufin, with tanwīn, declines the name in full, a licence of verse. kam fī jamālika Yūsufu, “how many a Joseph is in your beauty!”: every one of the youth's graces is a Joseph in itself. Line 12: the speaker is Maymūna, a jinniya: she whom the jinn fear trembles before a mortal youth. Line 13: takallafa, Form V, “to force oneself to”; mahāba, “awe”; ṣabā ilā, “to yearn toward”; jahda mā, “to the utmost of what”. Line 14: ṭarf aḥwar, an eye with ḥawar, the deep black of the iris against clear white; qiwām, “stature”; muhafhaf, “slender, light of waist”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ دَهْنَشُ شِعْرَ مَيْمُونَةَ فِي مَعْشُوقِهَا طَرِبَ غَايَةَ الطَّرَبِ وَتَعَجَّبَ كُلَّ الْعَجَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Dahnashu shiʿra Maymūnata fī maʿshūqihā ṭariba ghāyata al-ṭarabi wa-taʿajjaba kulla al-ʿajabi
sentences.l: So-when heard Dahnash (the) poetry (of) Maymūna about her-beloved, he-was-moved (to the) utmost (of) the-delight, and-he-marvelled all the-marvelling.
sentences.i: When Dahnash heard Maymūna's verses on her beloved, he was moved to the height of delight and wondered beyond all wonder.
sentences.n: ṭariba, “to be stirred to joy”, above all by music or verse. ghāyata al-ṭarabi and kulla al-ʿajabi strengthen each verb with its own noun: “the utmost of delight”, “all wonder”, a rhyming pair.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
